content: Quarterly Review of Film and Video, 32: 251–268, 2014 Copyright © Taylor & Francis Group, LLC ISSN: 1050-9208 print / 1543-5326 online DOI: 10.1080/10509208.2013.811354 Quiet American Imperialism: Euro-American Masculinity, Interracial Desire, and the Logic of Masculinist Protection in The Quiet American CORIE HARDY Phillip Noyce’s The Quiet American (2002), based on Graham Greene’s 1955 novel of the same name, begins with the following ominous lines spoken in voice-over by British actor Michael Caine: I can’t say what made me fall in love with Vietnam. That a woman’s voice can drug you? That everything is so intense. The colors, the taste, even the rain. . .They say whatever you’re looking for, you will ﬁnd here. . . You could be forgiven for thinking there was no war; that the gunshots were ﬁreworks; that only pleasure matters. A pipe of opium, or the touch of a girl who might tell you she loves you. And then, something happens, as you knew it would. And nothing can ever be the same again. Like many ﬁlmic representations of the Vietnam War (and Asia in general), The Quiet American’s interest lies not in depicting the Vietnamese people or their culture, but rather the role of Europeans and Euro-Americans “who lived, worked, and traveled in Asia” (Klein 10).1 This ethnocentric trend in American popular representations of the East is not surprising given both the historical fascination with and fear of the “alien” menace often referred to as “the yellow peril.” Rooted, as Gina Marchetti notes, “in medieval fears of Genghis Khan and Mongolian invasions of Europe” (2), the concept of the yellow peril “combines racist terror of alien cultures, sexual anxieties, and the belief that the West will be overpowered and enveloped by the irresistible, dark, occult forces of the East” (Marchetti 2). Since its inception in the late nineteenth century, this concept has fueled orientalist discourses and helped to maintain a binary opposition between East and West and, in turn, the Euro- American (i.e. white)2 “self” and the racialized (i.e. non-white) “Other.” Edward Said outlines the history and features of such discourses in his groundbreaking text, Orientalism. According to Said, the idea of the Orient itself was largely “a Euro- pean invention” (1), a way of expressing Western difference from and dominion over the East. Orientalism, then, is a discourse deeply embedded in power relations, speciﬁcally in European (and later, Euro-American) control over the Middle East and Asia. In short, orientalism provided a convenient justiﬁcation for European imperialism by constructing Corie Hardy is a Gender Studies PhD candidate (ABD) in the Women’s and Gender Studies program in the School of Social Transformation at Arizona State University. Her research interests include interracial intimacies, racial formation, intersectionality, and visual and narrative culture. 251

252 Corie Hardy the East as “irrational, backward-looking, childish, and feminine” (10) in contrast to the “rational, progressive, adult, and masculine” West (10). Orientalism not only asserts the supremacy of the West over the East by constructing Asia(ns) as inferior, however. In addition, as Michael Caine’s opening lines from The Quiet American illustrate, orientalist discourses conjure up eroticized and sexually charged images of the East as “a place of romance, exotic beings, haunting memories and landscapes, [and] remarkable experiences” (Said 1). This emphasis on the eroticism of the East led to fears regarding the “sexual danger of contact between the races” (Marchetti 3), a theme that I contend is still prevalent in contemporary popular attitudes toward and depictions of interracial intimacy in the United States. In this essay I consider one such representation, analyzing Graham Greene’s controver- sial anti-American Vietnam novel, The Quiet American (1955), as well as the subsequent ﬁlm adaptations of the book in 1958 and 2003. Through both a discursive analysis of these texts as well as a thorough an examination of the context(s) in which they were produced, I underscore the ways in which hegemonic Euro-American masculinity3 is constructed, in part, by nationalist ideologies and geopolitical processes that promote white male sex- ual access to Asian women. Furthermore, I highlight the discrepancies between Greene’s original novel, which critiqued U.S. involvement in Vietnam and the Cold War more gener- ally, Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s pro-American 1958 ﬁlm starring Audie Murphy and Michael Redgrave, and Phillip Noyce’s most recent take on the classic novel. Overall, I suggest that the popular depiction of interracial relationships between Euro- American men and Vietnamese women during the Vietnam War4 serves as a microcosm for the macro-level geopolitical processes and conﬁgurations that undergird American exceptionalism and what Iris Marion Young aptly identiﬁes as the “logic of masculinist protection,” ideologies that continue to reinforce a militant U.S. presence in Asia and the Middle East, particularly in the aftermath of September 11th. In addition, I argue that the prevalence of contemporary ﬁlms that revisit the Vietnam War era attempt to imply either a U.S. victory in Vietnam, or, at the very least, a legitimate reason for the American presence during the War. Given the immense unpopularity of the conﬂict, I contend that contemporary ﬁlms that allude to this era do so for explicitly political reasons, some of which include garnering public support for the so-called “war on terror,” uniting the American public against a “common enemy,” and championing Euro-American masculinity at the expense of gendered, racialized, and sexualized “Others.” Drawing on a post-colonial framework, I interrogate the interracial relationships at the center of The Quiet American and address the ways in which they are emblematic of both U.S. and European involvement in Vietnam and more loosely, contemporary tropes of European and Euro-American or white masculinity in the global arena. Before I explore these points, however, it is imperative to consider the historical context surrounding inter- racial intimacy in the United States, and particularly the strict regulation of Asian-white intimacies beginning in the 1860s with the arrival of Chinese laborers in the American West. “Haunted By Empire”: The Importance of Extra-Territorial Spaces to Asian/White Intimacies in the Twentieth Century and Beyond In “Mixing Bodies and Cultures: The Meaning of America’s Fascination with Sex Between ‘Orientals’ and ‘Whites’,” Henry Yu highlights the discursive construction of male Chinese, Japanese, and Filipino laborers in the American West throughout the mid-nineteenth and early-twentieth centuries as a menacing “yellow peril” or “Asiatic invasion” that had the

Quiet American Imperialism 253 potential to not only “overwhelm ‘white’ workers. . .[but] American civilization itself” (Yu 6). In addition to the hostility Asian-American men faced as workers, the widespread fear of the sexual prowess of ‘Oriental’ men was a chief concern of anti-Asian activists on the West Coast. This anxiety was illustrated in discursive representations of Asian-American men in pulp magazines, novels, and anti-Asian literature as “scheming” sexual predators “waiting in ambush to kidnap ‘white’ women into sexual slavery” (Yu 11–13). Mary Ti Ling Yui likewise notes that similar fears of interracial sexual contact between Chinese-American men and white women were extremely pervasive in and around the Chinatown district of turn-of-the-century New York City (Yui, 2005). Speciﬁcally, Lui highlights the racial and sexual anxieties surrounding the alleged murder of Elsie Sigel, a white woman, by Leon Ling, a Chinese-American man, in 1909. Although Sigel’s murder was never formally solved, in part because Leon Ling “disap- peared” after the crime,5 Yui suggests that the case further intensiﬁed white fears of the dangers of Chinatown and of the speciﬁc threat Chinese American men posed to white womanhood (Yui 9). Historian Peggy Pascoe also highlights—in contrast to the Leon Ling case—the sexual and racialized nature of stereotypes of Asian-Americans in the late-nineteenth century, explaining that “Chinese immigrant men were rarely depicted as direct sexual dangers to White women. Rather, images of fraudulent marriages, rampant prostitution, and commercial vice fostered the impression that Chinese immigrants were contagious purveyors of ‘deviant heterosexuality”’ (Pascoe 83). Asian-Americans were also discriminated against and discouraged from engaging in relationships with whites through legal measures such as the Page Law of 18756, the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, California’s Anti-Alien Land Acts of 1917 and 1923, various state-laws banning interracial marriage, and the Federal National Origins Act of 1924 (Yu 11). The passage and widespread support of these laws profoundly affected the lives and material realities of Asian-American men and women during this time, restricting Asian immigration, and more speciﬁcally, in the case of the Page Law and the Chinese Exclusion Act, the immigration of Chinese women to the United States. The absence of Chinese- American women made it virtually impossible for Chinese-American men to form families and thus “settle” in the United States, given the fact that anti-miscegenation laws throughout the west prohibited marriages between “whites” and “Chinese” or “Mongolians,” a term which Pascoe indicates was ﬁrst used in California in 1880 to describe Asian-Americans (84–85). In addition, policies of Chinese exclusion contributed to stereotypes of Asian- American women as prostitutes and “sex slaves” (85). In cases where Asian-American men and white women did manage to circumvent anti- miscegenation laws and legally marry, white women were constructed through newspaper articles and popular images as “deluded victims” under the spell of a “hypnotic trance” (Pascoe 91) that induced their attraction to Japanese-American and Chinese-American men. Popular representations of white women who married Asian and Asian-American men in New York City differed slightly, but also focused on the “helplessness” and moral depravity of such women. In The Chinatown Trunk Mystery, Yui argues that white women who married Chinese men were often perceived as poor, immoral, and drug-addicted (Yui 27). This was due, in part, to the widespread association of opium “dens” with the Chinese community. Yui notes that even though opium was a common ingredient in many drugs, smoking the substance directly was banned due to its association with the Chinese. According to Yui, “opium represented the racial and sexual transgressions” of the Chinese community and was therefore a constructed as a social threat (30–32). Both formal and informal restrictions on Asian-white interracial intimacy in the late 1800s and early 1900s illustrate the mutually constitutive relationship between discursive

254 Corie Hardy representations of Asian Americans as sexually deviant and immoral and the material realities of legal restrictions on immigration and marriage. Stereotypes of Asian-American men and women also invoked material consequences such as the surveillance and policing of Asian-owned businesses that were thought to be dangerous sites of interracial mixing and vice (Yui 48), the corralling of Asian-Americans into speciﬁc ethnic enclaves and neighborhoods (75), and “lynching, violence, and rioting against Asians” (Yu 12). Although relationships between Asian-American men and white women were both for- mally and informally discouraged well into the twentieth century, interracial relationships between Asian and Asian American women and Euro-American men were treated quite differently. In “Tiger Woods is Not the End of History: or, Why Sex across the Color Line Won’t Save Us All,” Henry Yu argues that anti-miscegenation laws banning Asian-white interracial intimacy in the western United States in the late-nineteenth and early-twentieth century “did nothing to deter white men from having sex with and at times marrying ‘Ori- ental’ women” (“Tiger Woods” 1412). Furthermore, Yu points to the “widespread sexual contact between American military personnel and sex workers who have serviced them throughout this century of wars in Asia and the Paciﬁc” (1412) as another gender-speciﬁc conﬁguration of interracial intimacy between Asians and Euro-Americans that was permit- ted, if not explicitly sanctioned, by the U.S. nation-state. “The importance of extraterritorial spaces to the management and production of white- Asian intimacies” (Koshy 10) is also emphasized by Susan Koshy in Sexual Naturalization: Asian Americans and Miscegenation. According to Koshy, most accounts of interracial in- timacy between Asians and Whites focus on relationships “within the. . .boundaries of the nation state” (10). This is problematic because, as Koshy indicates, the absence of what she terms “extraterritorial spaces” from historical studies of miscegenation is emblematic of “the state-bound cartographies of American history and the invisibility of American impe- rialism” (10). In the case of Chinese women, for example, Koshy notes that their exclusion from the United States (through measures such as the Page Law) “turned repeatedly on the potential threat signiﬁed by their sexuality,” which was overwhelmingly characterized as corrupt and disease-ridden (11). Paradoxically, the very same notion of Asian women’s “sexual immorality” also “heightened [their] allure” in non-U.S. locales, a fact that is consistent with Orientalist stereotypes of Asian women as “exotic” and “alluring” (Koshy 11). This particular contra- diction aptly illustrates the link between discursive representations of Asian women on the one hand and the twin material realities of their exclusion within the U.S. and their height- ened desirability (and sexual vulnerability and exploitation) in extraterritorial spaces on the other—a point that is particularly salient in light of this essay’s exploration of interracial intimacies sparked by the Cold War conﬂict in Vietnam. An additional contradiction lies in the fact that although sexual contact between white men and Asian women in such environments “emerged largely in the context of the sexual license and power afforded white men in treaty ports, military bases, or as occupying forces in Asia,” U.S. immigration policies “made marriage the precondition for the continuation of these relationships in the United States” (Koshy 11). Legislation such as the War Brides Act of 1945 was thus passed in order to allow Asian spouses of U.S. service members to enter the United States in spite of quotas that simultaneously restricted the majority of Asian immigration (11). Henry Yu notes that the racial “make-up” of pro-golfer Tiger Woods is illustrative of this particular trend, given the fact that his father, Earl Woods, served as a Green Beret during Vietnam and met his wife, Kultilda (Tiger Woods’ mother), while he was stationed in Thailand (“Tiger Woods” 1411). The relationship between Alden Pyle and Phuong in The Quiet American mirrors this trend, as it is Pyle’s intention to marry Phuong

Quiet American Imperialism 255 and take her back to the United States, an option that Fowler, an aging British journalist who already has a wife back home in Great Britain, cannot offer. White Supremacy and Racial Formation Theory In Racial Formation in the United States, Michael Omi and Harold Winant assert that “racial theory is shaped by actually existing race relations in any given historical period” (Omi and Winant 11). Such theories exist in order to provide society with “common sense” ideas about race (11). However, as Omi and Winant note, the dominant racial theory is subverted and replaced by a new theory whenever “it fails adequately to explain the changing nature of race relations, or when the racial policies it prescribes are challenged by political movements seeking a different arrangement” (11). This means that race is a socio-historical political process, and that dominant ideologies and beliefs about race are anything but “common sense”; rather, they are a product of power relations. For example, following the downfall of racial slavery in the United States, the dominant racial theory suggested a biologistic view of race in order to justify “racial inferiority as part of a natural order of humankind” (15). While the assertion that whites were biologically superior to non-whites was considered “common sense,” in reality this ideology was part of a desperate attempt to retain white supremacy after the abolition of slavery. In the 1920s and 1930s however, biologistic conceptions of race were challenged and replaced by what Omi and Winant refer to as the “ethnicity paradigm” (14), which suggests that racial categories are socially constructed.7 While a version of this racial theory is still accepted today, Omi and Winant contend that the recognition of race as a social construct did not (and has not) necessarily lead to equitable treatment for people of color in the United States. Rather, ethnicity theory “was solidly based in the framework of European (white) ethnicity” (16), which meant that racial minority groups were expected to assimilate to Euro-American standards. Many theorists and academics in ﬁelds such as whiteness studies and critical race theory have identiﬁed the simultaneous invisibility and pervasiveness of whiteness as an ideal (Alcoff 2005). Thus, while whites are constructed as normative and thus void of racial characterization, nonwhites are understood to “have” a race. However, historians such as David Roediger have revealed the ways in which many Americans who identify as “white” today would not have been able to do so a century ago, when many European immigrants who came to the United States, such as the Irish and the Italians, were classiﬁed as non-white, “dark,” and generally inferior (Roediger 4). While these groups were able to assimilate into the dominant white culture (largely at the expense of African Americans) by the mid-twentieth century, Roediger’s research reveals the instability, and indeed, im- purity of whiteness as a racial category despite the common perception of whiteness as a homogeneous, unexamined identity (Roediger 8–9). This historical context is undoubtedly important given the aims of this essay, posing critical questions regarding who is able to claim white privilege, as well how these notions of privilege translate into the arena of geopolitics to assert the superiority of the United States over the East following WWII, and speciﬁcally, during the conﬂict in Vietnam and throughout other Cold War struggles. Importantly, in their own theory of racial formation, Omi and Winant reject both the idea that race is an “essence” and the idea that race is an “illusion” (54). Rather, they suggest that race must be understood as “an unstable and ‘decentered’ complex of social meanings constantly being transformed by political struggle” (55). They go on to assert that “race is a concept which signiﬁes and symbolizes social conﬂicts and interests by referring to

256 Corie Hardy different types of human bodies” (55). As Henry Yu explains of the scholarly fascination with interracial relationships: The very conception of “intermarriage,” or contact between “races” and “cul- tures,” depend[s] upon the acceptance of a boundary that mark[s] the stark difference between one group and another. . .only in positing that there is a difference between two sets of people, and that this difference has great meaning, does someone come to be interested in examining the relations between people whom they deﬁne as different. (Yu 7) Similarly, in her analysis of interracial images in American popular culture, sociologist Erica Chito-Childs notes that “interracial sex and marriage represent a transgression of symbolic racial borders” (Chito-Childs 1; emphasis mine). Chito-Childs goes on to note that “only in a society where race is given primary importance do we even have couples socially constructed as interracial” (2). I emphasize this important—although arguably somewhat obvious—distinction be- cause the very practice of regulating interracial conﬁgurations of intimacy could not and would not exist without processes of racial formation and a “common sense” understand- ing of what it means to embody particular racial categories in a speciﬁc time and place. The variations in racial classiﬁcations available over the years in the U.S. census are il- lustrative of the ways in which racial categories—and therefore deﬁnitions of the term “interracial”—are malleable and subject to change (Hodes 240–270). Moreover, in ex- amining the many interracial relationships that have formed over the years as a result of U.S. involvement in “extraterritorial spaces,” a critical look at the ways in which racial formations are embedded in political conﬂicts and interests illuminates the power of ori- entalism as a strategic discourse and ideological formation in justifying U.S. imperialism and, speciﬁcally, the American presence in Vietnam. What is the relevance of these issues today? I argue that the ideologies of Euro- American hegemonic masculinity, which were informed by orientalist discourses and im- perialist desires, caused the United States to attempt a paternalistic “rescue mission” in Vietnam in order to save the South Vietnamese from their communist neighbors to the North. In many ways, it is possible to draw comparisons between the U.S. involvement in Vietnam and the current wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Again, U.S. forces are construed as attempting to “save” civilians in these regions of the Middle East from the barbarism of their own people.8 Again, the entire notion of the rescue narrative is predicated upon the assump- tion of Euro-American superiority, and in particular, the championing of Euro-American hegemonic masculinity. While much has been written about the mistakes made by Americans during the Vietnam War, it seems that there has been little interrogation of the underlying Cold War ideologies that caused U.S. forces to feel entitled to intervene, with or without the approval of the Vietnamese people, in the ﬁrst place. A notable exception is the work of Michael Hunt, a historian who has published extensively in the area of U.S. foreign policy, and speciﬁcally, on Vietnam. According to Hunt: We need. . .a framework that eschews superiority and inevitability and prompts both some degree of self-consciousness among Americans with a voice in the policy debate and a modicum of awareness about those supposedly arrayed

Quiet American Imperialism 257 against us and ostensibly teetering on the brink of barbarism or trapped in tradition. (Hunt 416) Hunt goes on to criticize what he deﬁnes as a “long-lived but perhaps hollow American nationalism quick to see evil, ready to combat barbarism, devoted to the advance of its way of life, and forgetful of a long record of U.S. intervention in the Middle East” (Hunt 416). However, one might contend that the majority of Americans would refuse to accept these assertions, given the continued use of the rhetoric of protection and “liberation” employed by the United States to ﬁght America’s “war on terror” (Hunt 2002; Altheide 2009). Similarly, the literary and ﬁlmic representations of interracial relationships between Euro-American men and Vietnamese women that I examine here provide examples of the Euro-American male desire to attempt an ethnocentric “civilizing mission” by “saving” a Vietnamese woman from her own oppressive culture. As I asserted in my introduction, the interracial romances that are at the center of these narratives are telling not only at the micro-level of race relations between intimate partners; they are also reﬂective of the large-scale geopolitical processes that deﬁne the tenuous relationship between East and West. In The Remasculinization of America: Gender and the Vietnam War, Susan Jeffords notes the immense popularity of representations of Vietnam in contemporary American culture. Through an analysis of “ﬁlms, personal narratives, criticism, novels, essays, and short stories” (xv), many of which were written by men who are themselves veterans of the war,9 Jeffords points to the disconnect between popular representations of U.S. involvement in Vietnam and the actual events that occurred during the war. She suggests that Vietnam veterans and others who have produced cultural representations of the war are engaged in the project of reclaiming American hegemonic masculinity by romanticizing and reconstructing the events of the war. Because gender ideology operates not just at the individual level but symbolically to represent the power of the nation, attempts to salvage the perception of the U.S.’s role in Vietnam are all the more vital. As scholar Thembisa Waetjen notes, “there is no denying that modern constructions of masculinity are bound up with the history of the nation-state and postcolonial independence, or that a conﬂation of civic and masculine virtues is at the heart of why soldiering, for example, is a male occupation” (Waetjen 127). While Waetjen focuses on the construction of masculinity in apartheid South Africa, her assertion that “accounting for men as gendered agents in nationalist processes” (127) is a task of great importance is certainly relevant in my analysis of contemporary popular ﬁlms that revisit Vietnam. What types of strategies do ﬁlmic representations of the Vietnam War employ to attempt to reclaim American masculinity? According to Jeffords, ﬁlms such as the Rambo series use techniques such as “the shift from ends to means, the proliferation of techniques and technologies, the valorization of [male] performance, the production and technologization of the male body as an aesthetic of spectacle, and the blurring of fact and ﬁction” (1) to celebrate American masculinity and to further the myth that America actually won the war. Rather than depicting the unpopularity of the war, these representations instead focus on the way that it was fought, thereby highlighting the prowess and expertise of the American soldier and suggesting that, if the war was lost, bureaucratic government operations, rather than individual soldiers, were to blame. Moreover, Jeffords points to the ways in which “Vietnam veterans are portrayed in contemporary American culture as emblems of an unjustly discriminated [against] masculinity” (116). She asserts that veterans of the war are portrayed as victims of a barrage of forces, including their own government,

258 Corie Hardy the war itself, the Vietnamese, American protestors, and the women’s movement (116). Thus, popular accounts of the war attempt to revive (white) American manhood and fuel a shift in American public opinion of the war and its soldiers. Moreover, it is imperative to draw attention to the fact that the cultural work that these representations do is incredibly racialized. Thus, while black and Latino soldiers constituted a signiﬁcant portion of the service members who fought in Vietnam, the majority of popular depictions of the war focus on white men. But, compared to Euro-American soldiers, a disproportionate number of soldiers of color engaged in heavy combat in Vietnam (Jeffords 29). Oliver Stone’s Born on the 4th of July, which stars Tom Cruise as American war veteran Ron Kovic, is but one of many popular ﬁlms that focuses exclusively on the experience of the Euro-American soldier both during and after the war. Two points are worth re-emphasizing regarding cultural representations of the war in Vietnam. The ﬁrst is that popular accounts of the war more often than not attempt to reframe and romanticize America’s role. Speciﬁcally, they suggest that the American presence in Vietnam was justiﬁed, and in the most heavily romanticized accounts, that the United States actually won the war. Second, the racial disparities that are evident in popular representations of Vietnam are reﬂective of the continued pervasiveness of U.S. white (male) privilege internationally. Originally set to open in theaters just weeks after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, the release of Phillip Noyce’s The Quiet American was delayed for more than a year due to concerns that the ﬁlm was too “anti-American” (PFS Film Review). Set in 1950s Vietnam, the ﬁlm focuses on the rivalry between aging British journalist Thomas Fowler (played by Michael Caine) and young American aid worker Alden Pyle (Brendan Fraser), both of whom are competing for the affections of a beautiful and young Vietnamese woman named Phuong (Do Thi Hai Yen). The most subversive aspect of the ﬁlm is its chilling subplot, which reveals the fact that Pyle is not, as he claims to be, a young American aid worker who has come to Vietnam to help the Vietnamese people. Rather, the audience later discovers that Pyle is actually part of an undercover operation responsible for making and setting off explosives with the aim of killing Vietnamese civilians. The purpose of this mission is to blame the attacks on the communists in order to garner support for the United States. In the ﬁnal climatic scene of the movie between Pyle and Fowler, Fowler confronts Pyle, who admits to his role in the explosives operation and idealistically proclaims, “In the end, I’m going to save lives.” When Fowler cautions Pyle to think of Phuong and what he is doing to her people, Pyle simply responds by claiming that his affection for Phuong only makes him more committed to his cause. Pyle’s paternalistic10 desire to “save” the Vietnamese people also is reﬂected in his romantic interest in Phuong. Although he ﬁrst meets the young Vietnamese woman through Fowler, who is her boyfriend, Pyle appears to be immediately enamored by his new ac- quaintance. He asks Fowler about Phuong’s past and Fowler informs him that while she came from a “good” family, after the death of her father Phuong was forced to become a taxi dancer, a type of dance hostess commonly found in saloons and dance halls.11 At such establishments, men could request a dance or the companionship of a woman through the purchase of a ticket or a drink. As Pyle remarks in The Quiet American, the Asian women who took up this type of employment were perceived as roughly akin to prostitutes. Once Pyle becomes aware of the fact that Fowler has a wife back in England and thus cannot marry Phuong, he approaches Fowler and expresses his interest in the young woman. Interestingly, there is little mention of Phuong’s desire, but rather a discussion between the two men regarding who is better suited to “take care” of her. Pyle contends that he “never

Quiet American Imperialism 259 used to believe in love at ﬁrst sight.” However, referring to an earlier scene in the ﬁlm where he and Fowler witnessed the desperation of a group of Vietnamese prostitutes in a “House of Girls,” Pyle confesses that “after seeing those other girls in that awful place and thinking that Phuong could easily become one of them, I want to protect her.” Pyle does not express any interest in Phuong’s feelings about the matter. Instead, he sees himself as the practical choice since Fowler cannot marry her and since, as a result of living with Fowler, a European man, she can “never have a proper marriage to a Vietnamese man.” Pyle’s conﬁdent proclamation that he is better suited to care for Phuong exempliﬁes his orientalist and paternalistic mindset. In addition, in comparison to the middle-aged Fowler, who is at least twenty to thirty years Phuong’s senior, Pyle exhibits a more desirable and assertive, or hegemonic, brand of masculinity. Indeed, in the scene where Pyle comes to Fowler and Phuong’s home to offer Phuong his protection, Fowler appears completely impotent and makes no attempt to stop Pyle or offer any kind of protest. The positioning of the actors is also reﬂective of this power dynamic. While Fowler and Phuong both sit, Pyle stands over them making his case. While obviously upset that Pyle is trying to lay claim to “his girl” (as he later refers to Phuong), Fowler accepts his position as subordinate to Pyle’s by allowing him to come into his home and propose to Phuong. His insecurities are conﬁrmed when, after Phuong (initially) denies Pyle and he leaves the apartment, Fowler remarks “He’s very young.” Phuong attempts to reassure Fowler and replies, “that’s not so important.” However, Fowler’s very mention of the age difference between himself and Pyle indicates that he sees Pyle as possessing certain advantages over him. The conﬂict between Pyle and Fowler reﬂects the larger shift in power that occurred between Great Britain and the United States following WWII, when the U.S. replaced Britain as a world super power. As Said notes, “From the beginning of the nineteenth century until the end of World War II France and Britain dominated the Orient and Orientalism; since World War II America has dominated the Orient, and approaches it as France and Britain once did” (Said 4). This geopolitical shift is mirrored in the ﬁlm through the literal transfer of Phuong from the aging British Fowler to the young and powerful Pyle, who both view Phuong through the lens of orientalist discourse. The conﬂation of Phuong with the Orient, and more speciﬁcally, Vietnam, is clearly stated by Fowler early in the ﬁlm as he expresses, in voiceover, his regret at introducing Phuong and Pyle. Although at this point Fowler has not yet introduced Pyle to his lover, Fowler speaks as an omniscient narrator from his location in the present. He remarks: “I should have realized how saving a country and saving a woman could be the same thing to someone like Pyle.” The construction of Phuong as an object whose only importance lies in her exchange value is emphasized throughout the ﬁlm. Fowler ﬁrst refers to Phuong in this context when Pyle visits their apartment to profess his love to Phuong. “Let’s toss for her,” Fowler casually suggests, as if the decision as to whom Phuong should be with (1) does not belong to Phuong and (2) can be easily decided by something as simple as the ﬂip of a coin. This suggestion dehumanizes Phuong and reﬂects her lack of agency in the exchange. While she is present in the room, she does not speak or interfere in the argument. Fowler again treats Phuong as a possession after he and Pyle survive a life threatening attack in North Vietnam. “If I had died,” Fowler tells Pyle, “you could have had her.” As Gayle Rubin notes in “The Trafﬁc in Women,” “if it is women who are being transacted, then it is the men who give and take them who are linked, the woman being a conduit of a relationship rather than a partner to it” (Rubin 37). The Quiet American is perhaps then a ﬁlm more about the masculine bond (and its ultimate unraveling) between Fowler and Pyle than about either of the men’s intimacy with Phuong.

260 Corie Hardy Both Pyle and Fowler’s yearning for Phuong seems to have little to do with whom she is as a person, or any of her speciﬁc character traits. Phuong is, in actuality, a minor character in the ﬁlm, garnering little screen time in comparison to both Fowler and Pyle. Following Rubin’s analysis, Phuong is therefore “in no position to realize the beneﬁts of [her] own circulation” (Rubin 37). Desirable simply because of the orientalist ideals she represents, Phuong is constructed as exotic, mysterious, and fragile—a commodity rather than a unique and individual person. As bell hooks notes, the idea that “there is pleasure to be found in. . .the enjoyment of racial difference” is prevalent in contemporary mass culture. hooks asserts that: The commodiﬁcation of Otherness has been so successful because it is offered as a new delight, more intense, more satisfying than normal ways of doing and feeling. Within commodity culture, ethnicity becomes a spice, seasoning that can liven up the dull dish that is mainstream white culture. (hooks 21) In The Quiet American, hooks’ points seem particularly relevant. Thomas Fowler is con- structed as a rather boring man in a loveless marriage with a European woman. He is older, relatively unproductive as a journalist, and seemingly set in his ways. Phuong appears, then, to be the only exciting or valuable aspect of his life. He admits this about halfway through the ﬁlm as he confesses to Pyle that if he were to lose Phuong, for him it would be “the beginning of death.” While this is perhaps an acknowledgement of his vulnerability, Fowler’s desire for Phuong is also steeped in the discourses of conquest or “the chase.” This is revealed in an early scene of the movie when Fowler explains to Pyle that he ﬁrst met Phuong when she was a taxi dancer in a club catering to Euro-American visitors in Vietnam. While Pyle assumes that Fowler was easily able to “woo” Phuong, Fowler objects, exclaiming “Good God, no! It took me six months to get her to go on a date.” Similarly, Pyle appears to be a dull and relatively average man. In fact, he is the ﬁlm’s title character; the “quiet” American. It is likely, then, that he not only wishes to “protect” Phuong and care for her in a paternalistic sense, but that he desires to “consume” her as a way of “experiencing” his idea of the eroticized Orient. In his ﬁrst meeting with Phuong, Pyle compliments her, asserting “Phuong is a very beautiful name.” Phuong tells Pyle that her name means “phoenix.” Surprised, Pyle replies “I thought it meant ﬂower, like the ones in your hair.” In this scene Pyle literally redeﬁnes Phuong according to his own stereotypical understanding of the Asian woman as lotus ﬂower—the loyal, self-sacriﬁcing, subservient Asian woman (Parre˜nas Shimizu 20). Thus it is evident from this ﬁrst interaction that Pyle values Phuong for what she represents, rather than who she is. Within the context of the ﬁlm, it is impossible to gauge Phuong’s response to the events that take place. She is largely a silent actor, standing by as the two men ﬁght over her. In his review of the ﬁlm, critic Roger Ebert characterizes Phuong as “a dance hall girl.” He notes that she loves Fowler “because he pays her to,” an arrangement that “suits them both” (Ebert). This does indeed appear to be the case. While Phuong does not speak for much of the ﬁlm, the one point she does reiterate is her desire to marry Fowler. While he cannot marry her because his English wife refuses to grant him a divorce, Phuong’s repeated desire to be wed indicates her desire for economic security and social respectability. In one of the ﬁrst scenes of the ﬁlm between Fowler and Phuong, he remarks “I’d marry you if I could. You know that.” Phuong answers “yes” and then hopefully asks “You think your wife will give divorce?” Fowler discouragingly replies that he doesn’t think so, but after Pyle’s proposal to Phuong later in the ﬁlm, Fowler writes home to his wife to ask for a divorce anyway.

Quiet American Imperialism 261 While her answer is no, Fowler lies to Phuong and says that his wife has agreed. When Phuong discovers that this is not the case, she barges into the apartment with Pyle to confront Fowler. However, Phuong barely speaks. Although she is the one who has been betrayed, the entire exchange takes place between the two men. At the end of the conversation, Pyle protectively says “Come on, Phuong,” and she silently exits the apartment, leaving with Pyle. It is impossible to tell in this scene what Phuong’s desires are. She complies and goes with Pyle, but her motivation for doing so is unclear. While it is possible that Phuong feels hurt and betrayed by Fowler, it is equally likely that she leaves him because she sees Pyle as the more reliable and secure choice between the two men. In either case, love does not seem to enter into the equation. Phuong’s choices are constructed, rather, as a matter of practicality. Gender relations in The Quiet American are reﬂective of the wartime relationship between America as a masculine, dominant world power and Vietnam as a feminized, invaded country. While the ﬁlm is critical of the United States in that it portrays Americans engaging in terrorist acts, the element of interracial romance in the ﬁlm continues to afﬁrm the supremacy of the Euro-American male subject. Moreover, given that Fowler is presented as the “leading man” of the ﬁlm, his triumph over Pyle, the “villain,” allows white masculinity to save face. Fowler thus emerges at the end of the ﬁlm as the hero who punishes Pyle and rescues Phuong from the life of a dance hall girl by promising to stay by her side in Vietnam rather than return to his wife in his native England. What is the salience of a ﬁlm like The Quiet American in this particular historical moment? Given that the ﬁlm was released just a year after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in the United States, it is impossible to ignore the parallels between The United States’ past involvement in Vietnam and its current investment in areas of the Middle East such as Iraq and Afghanistan. According to Iris Marion Young, since the September 11th attacks the American government operates according to “a logic of masculinist protec- tion,” which stipulates that citizens must be willing to relinquish some of their freedoms in exchange for protection from outside attacks (Young 2). This justiﬁcation, used to sup- port measures such as the Patriot Act (which has been harshly criticized for infringing upon Americans’ right to privacy), requires that those in the protected position (namely, women and children) accept their placement in a “subordinate position of dependence and obedience” (Young 2). This rationale is not only used to legitimize government control over the domestic population and to garner support for warfare; it is also expanded to justify invasion as a civilizing mission to “liberate” the “oppressed” people of a particular country. For example, when the United States began bombing Afghanistan in late 2001 as a response to the September 11th attacks (despite a lack of evidence that the country was actually involved), the American government justiﬁed these actions by claiming that Afghanistan was an active supporter of al-Qaeda. Perhaps because this claim was weak, Young notes that “the United States quickly repackaged the war as a case of humanitarian intervention to liberate the Afghan people” (Young 17). In particular, the Bush adminis- tration focused their efforts on the protection of women. In the 2002 State of the Union address, Bush claimed “The last time we met in this chamber the mothers and daughters of Afghanistan were captives in their own homes, forbidden from working or going to school” (Young 17). While advocating for greater rights for women is certainly a worthy cause, the fact that American feminists unsuccessfully attempted to draw attention to the treatment of women by the Taliban in the years before Sept. 11th suggests that the “appeal to women’s rights was a cynical attempt to gain support for the war among the citizens of the United States and other liberal countries” (Young 18).

262 Corie Hardy The current state of America’s involvement in countries such as Iraq and Afghanistan mirrors the same strategies used during the U.S. occupation of wartime Vietnam. Intent on “saving” the South Vietnamese from the communists to the North, America justiﬁed their pervasive presence in the country. And within The Quiet American, just as in Iraq and Afghanistan, Pyle appeals to women’s rights as a central justiﬁcation for his work in Vietnam. This point is made explicit when Pyle explains his desire to save Phuong from her circumstances. Explaining his actions to Fowler, Pyle says “Let’s just look at Phuong. There’s beauty. There’s the daughter of a professor. Taxi dancer. Mistress of an older European man. That pretty well describes the whole country. Look, Thomas, we are here to save Vietnam from all of that.” The “we” of Pyle’s statement, the American masculinist presence in the global arena, is at work again today. Thus, The Quiet American, when read as a critique of the U.S. as a global power (as it was intended to be in the original Greene novel) has a great deal of relevance as a twenty-ﬁrst century ﬁlm that provides a much needed window into a past we are dangerously close to repeating. On the other hand, the more recent ﬁlm is disquieting in its relative silence about the Cold War context, which was so critical to Greene’s 1955 novel and Mankiewicz’s 1958 (albeit signiﬁcantly altered) ﬁlm adaptation. As Robert J. McMahon notes, “the im- mediate roots of the Cold War, at least in broad, structural terms, lay in the intersection between a world rendered prostrate by a devastating global conﬂict [WWII] and the con- ﬂicting recipes for international order that Washington and Moscow sought to impose on that pliable, war shattered world” (McMahon 5). In other words, the Cold War was born out of the aftermath of both the First and Second World Wars, in which the Soviet Union and the United States emerged with two very different approaches to restoring the global postwar order. While the U.S. suffered “relatively moderate losses” in compar- ison to the Soviets, both countries expressed a strong interest in national defense, and especially in the case of the Soviet Union, prohibiting any future attempts at territorial invasions through Poland and other surrounding countries (McMahon 10–11). Moreover, as McMahon illustrates, “ideology imparted to Soviets and Americans alike a messianic faith in the world-historical roles of their respective nations. On each side. . .leaders and ordinary citizens saw their countries acting for much broader purposes than the mere advancement of national interests” (15). Indeed, the tenuous wartime alliance between the United States, the world’s leading capitalist power, and the Soviet Union, its “chief proponent of international proletariat revolution” (16), was, in retrospect, destined for failure. More speciﬁcally, the impending conﬂict between the U.S. and Vietnam was foreshad- owed as early as 1919 when Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh was excluded, despite his enthusiasm for U.S. President Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points, from peace proceedings in Versailles. Disillusioned, Ho later sided with the French Communist Party in light of their support for “immediate independence for all colonial areas” (Kirkpatrick). Ho quickly became a leading voice in the party and travelled throughout Europe and Indochina until his return to Vietnam in the early 1940s. He subsequently went on to lead the Viet Minh against French colonial forces, culminating in a Vietnamese victory in 1954 at the battle of Dien Bien Phu (Kirkpatrick). “The epic struggles for national freedom and indepen- dence mounted by Asia and other Third World peoples in the aftermath of World War II,” McMahon writes, “rank among the most powerful historical forces of the 20th century” (McMahon 36). Although these struggles likely would have taken place with or without the Cold War, their simultaneous occurrence fated the two to become “inextricably linked, each shaping and being shaped by the other” (36) a phenomenon that is particularly visible in the context of Vietnam.

Quiet American Imperialism 263 It is precisely this context, however, that is missing from Noyce’s 2002 version of The Quiet American, a ﬁlm that many critics have noted seems to warn of the later events of the war much more so than Greene’s novel or Mankiewicz’s 1958 ﬁlm, an observation that makes sense considering that both were conceived prior to America’s disastrous in- volvement in what would come to be known as the Second Indochina War. Noyce’s ﬁlm is perhaps more provocative for the ways in which it resonated in the immediate aftermath of the September 11th attacks than for its faithful adherence to Greene’s novel and the ideological struggles of the Cold War. The 2002 ﬁlm, in fact, came very close to not being released in American theaters at all. It was only at the urging of one of the ﬁlm’s stars, British actor Michael Caine, that producer Harvey Weinstein reluctantly showed the ﬁlm at the 2002 Toronto Film Festival, where it received rave reviews and went on to garner Caine an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor (Beck). The 2002 adaptation of the narrative departs most from Greene’s vision in its portrayal of Alden Pyle, the title character, as a sinister and culpable villain who clearly articulates his motives and admits he will stop at nothing to “save” Vietnam from the communist threat. In contrast, Greene’s Pyle is a caricature, a tirelessly idealistic and “innocent” man who truly has noble intentions but “turns murderous in his feckless ignorant scheming” (Stone xv). As Robert Stone notes in his introduction to the 2004 edition of the novel, even the title of Greene’s narrative is a joke, given that the American is not quiet at all, but rather, a “prattling fool” (Stone vii). The joke’s “unspoken punch line,” according to Stone, is that “the only quiet American is a dead American” (vii). Needless to say, this characterization did not sit well with American audiences in 1955, and while the 2002 ﬁlm was not universally well-received due to its anti-American slant, perhaps what is most offensive about Greene’s characterization of Pyle is his utter stupidity, which Greene kindly characterizes as American “innocence.” In one particularly telling passage, the book’s protagonist, British journalist Thomas Fowler (believed to be a thinly veiled version of Greene himself) reﬂects on Pyle’s trou- blesome character ﬂaw, musing “what’s the good? He’ll always be innocent, you can’t blame the innocent, they are always guiltless. All you can do is control or eliminate them. Innocence is a kind of insanity” (Greene 155). However, in Noyce’s 2002 adaptation, Pyle (played by Brendan Fraser) is quite matter-of-fact in his conviction that some Vietnamese must die in order to gain the ideological footing necessary to stop communist forces and declare an American victory in Vietnam. While in the novel’s climatic scene, in which a bomb decimates the central square of Saigon, Pyle reacts with shock and horror at the devastation around him, in the 2002 version of the ﬁlm Fraser’s character responds with an air of detached pragmatism, calming wiping the blood off of his pants leg and shoes because, as he states, he must “get them cleaned” before he sees the general. Largely absent of the Cold War context that made the novel such a chilling and accurate prediction of events that were still to come, the most recent iteration of The Quiet American portrays a hyper-masculinized and brutish America willing to go to any lengths in order to quell ideological unrest and restore global order and the American way of life. At the same time the enemy in the 2002 ﬁlm is somehow more diffuse. Whereas Greene’s novel clearly condemns the American for his ignorance and reveals the ways in which the fear of the spread of communism led America to attempt to “inﬂict its will in a part of the world to whose language and gestures it was tone deaf” (Stone xviii), Noyce’s ﬁlm reads like an intriguing mystery that the viewer never manages to fully solve. In this version of the story it is unclear exactly who Pyle works for or what enemy or ideology he is so intent on conquering, whereas both Greene’s novel and the 1958 ﬁlm adaptation are much clearer on the American’s anti-communist stance, his strident belief in a “Third

264 Corie Hardy force”12 with the potential to “liberate” the country (i.e. institute an American way of life), and his (and many others’) worry that the spread of communism to one Asian country would kick off a “domino” effect, in which all others would soon follow. Again, in the absence of the Cold War context in which the original book and ﬁrst ﬁlm were both couched, these discrepancies are understandable. In an age where U.S. imperial efforts are both more sophisticated and less overt (a lesson which the conﬂict in Vietnam arguably taught us), confusion regarding who is ﬁghting whom and for what purposes is virtually a necessity. In the case of the current “war on terror,” as Iris Marion Young and many others have repeatedly noted, justiﬁcations for the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan have been numerous, and yet, ultimately unsatisfying, as there remains no clear connection between these territories and the 2001 attack on the United States (Young). The Vietnamese in Noyce’s ﬁlm receive little screen time and function largely as a stand-in for the Iraqi and Afghan people. Even Phuong, the love interest of both Fowler and Pyle and the ﬁlm’s only central Vietnamese character, has nothing to say about the conﬂict; she merely exists, sheltered in a child-like world of milkshakes and gossip magazines (which seem, sadly, to be her only two interests.) Mankiewicz’s 1958 ﬁlm emphasizes this point most clearly in a scene where the young, idealistic Pyle claims he wants to “take care” of Phuong and give her a better “future,” a point which is refuted by Fowler, who quickly informs him that she “does not understand” such abstractions, but merely wants to survive. Despite this admission, in both the novel and the 1958 ﬁlm Fowler clearly views Phuong as disposable, while the in new version of the ﬁlm he confesses to Pyle that were he to lose Phuong, for him it would be a kind of death. As with the various representations of Pyle’s character, the construction of Phuong and the portrayal of her relationships with both Fowler and Pyle in the various versions of the narrative mirror the larger shifts in both the American and British presence in the contemporary transnational arena. The romance at the heart of The Quiet American is easily glossed over when we consider the ways in which it represents the large scale geopolitical processes, nationalist ideologies, and constructions of masculinity that shape our understanding of America’s role in the Vietnam War. In the novel and both ﬁlm adaptations of The Quiet American, the interracial intimacy between Phuong and Fowler (and brieﬂy, Phuong and Pyle) is easy to overlook because the audience sees so little of it. The most intimate moment in the 2002 ﬁlm is the ﬁrst scene containing both Phuong and Fowler. Fowler enters his apartment to ﬁnd a small gift on the bed. When he walks over to pick it up, Phuong sneaks up behind him and exclaims, in her characteristic broken English, “Today our anniversary! Did you forget?” Fowler remarks that he cannot believe it has been two years already. He lies down on the bed and Phuong climbs on top of him. The scene ends with a shot of Phuong’s back as she removes her shirt and then lies down on top of Fowler. The way this scene is shot is notable for its construction of Phuong as both dominant and submissive at the same time. While she acts as the aggressor by climbing on top of Fowler and removing her blouse, her demeanor is very innocent and child-like, as evidenced through her high-pitched voice, angelic facial expressions, and broken English. Moreover, in the scene Fowler jokingly cautions Phuong to be careful when she climbs into bed with him because he is “old and fragile.” Thus, her position as dominant in their (implied) sexual encounter appears to be out of service to the aging Fowler rather than a desire to take charge in the bedroom. In contrast, both Greene’s novel and Mankiewicz’s ﬁlm present a thoroughly sanitized view of the relationship, with no depiction of intimacy between the characters at all. In these versions of the story Phuong barely seems to matter except for the competition between the two men, which she represents. For example, although Fowler expresses his

Quiet American Imperialism 265 fear of losing Phuong in the 2002 ﬁlm when Pyle comes to him to profess his love for her, in Mankiewicz’s Quiet American Fowler appears to have little emotional connection to his Vietnamese lover, conﬁdently asserting “I intend to keep her. . .I’d rather ruin her and be with her than worry about her interests.” Similarly, in the novel Fowler makes a comparable statement, admitting “I don’t care for her interests. You can have her interests. I only want her body. I want her in bed with me.” The contrast between Michael Caine’s embodiment of masculinity in 2002 and Michael Redgrave’s in 1958 is striking. Redgrave’s performance is largely detached and unemotional, and it seems, despite his annoyance with the American, that he will be just ﬁne with or without Phuong in his life. Caine however, literally breaks down and sobs at the moment when he loses Phuong to Pyle, his vulnerability and feebleness on display at virtually every turn. The vast difference in age between the two actors is also telling, as Redgrave was just ﬁfty years old when he portrayed Fowler, whereas Caine was nearly seventy. These distinctions highlight the striking differences during the respective eras in which the ﬁlms were made. While Europe was just beginning to lose its colonial footholds in Vietnam and Indochina more broadly in the late 1950s, in 2002 following the September 11th attacks on the United States many Americans condemned the reluctance of European countries such as France and Great Britain to become involved in the impending conﬂict. Caine’s portrayal of Fowler seems to lament the fall of the once powerful past empire, relying on a deeply feminine and racialized construction of masculinity. In contrast, Redgrave’s performance is strong and self assured, his character much more conﬁdent and intelligent in comparison to Audie Murphy’s portrayal of the blundering, idiotic American—who, it is worth noting, is truly innocent in this much loathed ﬁlmic adaptation of the story, in which Pyle is not a terrorist but a simple toy-maker whom Fowler mistakes for evil. Perhaps what is most notable about the interracial romance in The Quiet American is that neither Fowler nor Phuong ever actually verbalize their affection for one another. While in one scene in the 2002 version Fowler tells Pyle that losing Phuong would be “the beginning of death” for him, neither Fowler nor Phuong actually say the words “I love you” to one another. Given the economic and social wages of her relationship with Fowler, it is highly possible that to Phuong it does not matter if she loves Fowler, or any man, only that she is taken care of. However, it is unfortunately impossible to gauge her feelings, as there is so little development of Phuong’s character in the novel or either of the subsequent ﬁlms. In Mankiewicz’s 1958 version, Phuong is not even played by a Vietnamese (or even Asian!) actress, but rather the Italian beauty Giorgia Moll. Even in Greene’s novel, Phuong is an essentially ﬂat character, and although her presence complicates Fowler’s motivation for “taking sides” and deciding to eliminate Pyle, the story is much more about the contest between the two men—and by extension, two competing Cold War ideologies—than it is about vying for a woman’s (or a country’s) affection. What are the implications of America’s continued obsession with re-writing the events of the Vietnam War in ways that parallel our strategic investment in territories such as Afghanistan and Iraq? I have argued here that Noyce’s 2002 adaptation of Greene’s classic novel departs from its predecessor(s) in signiﬁcant ways, largely because the Cold War context that made the original novel and the 1958 ﬁlm so relevant no longer exists. Rather, Noyce’s vision has much more cultural currency in the aftermath of September 11th and two global wars on terror. While this modern take on the story is often praised for preserving the original anti-American bend of the novel, unlike the 1958 ﬁlm, in many ways it also champions white American masculinity and by extension, the cause of the United States more broadly in the global “war on terror.”

266 Corie Hardy While both Greene and Mankiewicz characterize Pyle as a blundering fool, Noyce gives him much more credit for his intentions, portraying in a very straightforward manner the “quiet” American’s (note that there is no irony in this phrase in the contemporary version of the tale) strident belief that some must die and compromises must be made in order to achieve a greater good. Although murderous in his intentions, many Americans might agree with Pyle that the suffering of a few is permissible in order to achieve the protection of many, particularly when the few are racialized and gendered subjects who, like Phuong, have little say in the matter. This is perhaps the most frightening aspect of the popularity and critical acclaim that Noyce’s ﬁlm has garnered, especially when placed within the larger cannon of post-9/11 war ﬁlms that simultaneous highlight the horrors and injustices of war while afﬁrming the necessity of such struggles.13 Notes 1.
